facts.explanation: In the early days of microchips, Gordon Moore noticed that the number of transistors that fit on a chip kept doubling at a steady pace. Starting from Intel's first microprocessor and doubling every two years lands remarkably close to the biggest chips made decades later.

facts.query: If the history of technology were squeezed into one day, when would computers appear?
facts.topic: History of technology in one day
facts.explanation: Squeeze the whole story of human technology, from the first chipped stones to the smartphone, into a single day ending at midnight. Stone tools fill almost the entire day; writing and the wheel arrive only in the final minutes, and every electronic invention crowds into the last fraction of a second.

facts.label: Oldest known stone tools
facts.description: Hominins at Lomekwi, Kenya, knap the oldest stone tools yet found, about 3.3 million years ago.
facts.sourceNote: Harmand et al., Nature, 2015 (Lomekwi 3 site, Kenya)

facts.label: The wheel
facts.description: Wheels appear in Mesopotamia, first for pottery and soon after for carts, around 3500 BCE.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica, history of technology

facts.label: Writing
facts.description: Sumerian scribes in Mesopotamia begin writing in cuneiform around 3200 BCE.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica, history of technology

facts.label: Gutenberg's printing press
facts.description: Johannes Gutenberg develops movable-type printing in Mainz around 1440.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica, history of technology

facts.label: Newcomen steam engine
facts.description: Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine starts pumping water from a mine in England.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica, history of technology

facts.label: Telephone patented
facts.description: Alexander Graham Bell is granted his telephone patent.
facts.sourceNote: US Patent 174,465; Library of Congress

facts.label: ENIAC unveiled
facts.description: ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, is shown to the public in Philadelphia.
facts.sourceNote: Smithsonian Institution; University of Pennsylvania

facts.label: Transistor invented
facts.description: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley demonstrate the first transistor at Bell Labs.
facts.sourceNote: Nokia Bell Labs history; Nobel Prize in Physics 1956

facts.label: First microprocessor
facts.description: Intel announces the 4004, the first commercial single-chip microprocessor.
facts.sourceNote: Intel Corporation, Intel 4004 product history

facts.label: World Wide Web proposed
facts.description: Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web at CERN.
facts.sourceNote: CERN, history of the Web

facts.label: iPhone goes on sale
facts.description: Apple's first iPhone goes on sale in the United States.
facts.sourceNote: Apple Inc. press release, June 2007

plan.title: The history of technology in one day
plan.caption: From the first stone tools to the smartphone; now is midnight.

facts.query: How does a rocket reach orbit?
facts.explanation: Getting to orbit is less about going up than about going sideways fast enough to keep falling around the Earth instead of back onto it. A rocket climbs out of the thick lower atmosphere, then tips over and spends most of its fuel building horizontal speed, dropping empty stages along the way.

facts.label: Liftoff
facts.title: Liftoff
facts.description: The engines burn propellant and push exhaust downward; once thrust exceeds the rocket's weight, it rises off the pad.
facts.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets

facts.label: Gravity turn
facts.title: Pitch over
facts.description: Shortly after clearing the tower, the rocket tilts and lets gravity gradually bend its path toward the horizontal.
facts.sourceNote: NASA, launch vehicle ascent trajectory guides

facts.label: Maximum dynamic pressure
facts.title: Max Q
facts.description: Air pressure on the speeding rocket peaks as it climbs through the lower atmosphere; engines are often throttled back to limit stress.
facts.sourceNote: NASA Space Shuttle mission ascent summaries

facts.label: Stage separation
facts.title: Staging
facts.description: The first stage burns out and drops away so the rocket no longer carries its empty tanks; the upper stage ignites.
facts.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Rockets

facts.label: Fairing jettison
facts.title: Nose cone opens
facts.description: Once above most of the air, the protective fairing around the payload splits off to save weight.
facts.sourceNote: NASA Launch Services Program, mission overviews

facts.label: Building orbital speed
facts.title: Go sideways, fast
facts.description: The upper stage burns almost horizontally until the vehicle is fast enough that the ground curves away as quickly as it falls.
facts.sourceNote: NASA, What is an orbit? (NASA Knows)

facts.label: Engine cutoff and payload release
facts.title: Orbit
facts.description: The engine shuts down on the planned orbit and the satellite or spacecraft separates to begin its mission.
facts.sourceNote: NASA Launch Services Program, mission overviews

facts.query: How small are the features on a computer chip?
facts.topic: From a silicon crystal to a wafer
facts.explanation: Modern chips are carved from discs of pure silicon using light. Chipmakers switched to extreme ultraviolet light, with a wavelength only a few dozen silicon crystal cells across, to print features far thinner than a human hair, across a wafer as wide as a dinner plate.
